claims.text: The degree of local lattice distortion governs premelting and melting behavior in HEA nanoparticles.
Nanoscale chemical segregation governs premelting and melting behavior in HEA nanoparticles.
Local compositional inhomogeneity produces spatially varying cohesive energies.
Local compositional inhomogeneity produces spatially varying surface energies.
Contrasts in local cohesive and surface energies promote thin premelted surface layers at lower temperatures than in a homogeneous, less-distorted baseline.
Rapid solidification can maintain nearly homogeneous mixing of the constituent elements in HEA nanoparticles.
Controlled annealing can induce slight nanoscale elemental segregation in HEA nanoparticles.
The proposed annealing treatment increases local lattice distortion.
Surface segregation of lower-melting-point elements modulates nanoparticle surface energy.
Surface segregation of lower-melting-point elements drives earlier onset of a premelted state.
Differences in atomic sizes and interaction energies create heterogeneous distributions of bonding strength within HEA nanoparticles.
Regions with enhanced lattice distortion have lower local melting barriers.
Chemically segregated regions have lower local melting barriers.
Lower local melting barriers cause earlier formation of a disordered premelted surface layer.
A more uniform elemental distribution produces a higher and more spatially uniform melting barrier.
Segregated HEA nanoparticles will begin premelting at significantly lower temperatures than homogeneous nanoparticles.
The premelting onset temperature of segregated nanoparticles could be 10–20% lower than that of the homogeneous baseline.
The predicted premelted layer will be detectable through structural and compositional changes using in-situ TEM.
The proposed relationship should hold for HEA nanoparticles between 5 and 50 nm over typical multi-principal-element alloy compositions.
The proposed relationship may not extend to bulk HEAs or to systems with dramatically different chemistries.
